source.title: Weak-to-Strong Preference Optimization: Stealing Reward from Weak Aligned Model
source.authors: Wen-Hong Zhu; Zhi-Wei He; Xiaofeng Wang; Pengfei Liu; Rui Wang

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper, appendices, tables, and example generations are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether alignment information from a weaker model can improve a stronger model, but uses WSPO, which transfers distribution differences rather than the original weak-label fine-tuning method, and does not report PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for weak-to-strong alignment transfer and comparisons with SFT and DPO. It does not report PGR or a strong model trained on true labels as a ceiling. Cited results from other work and example generations are not recorded as result rows.
record.test_reason: WSPO trains a 7B/8B student on a supervisory signal from an aligned 1.5B/1B model, its log-prob ratio before and after alignment. It reports the student's alignment scores next to the weak supervisor's scores on the same benchmarks (Tables 1, 6, 7, 10). That bears on V1 with a different method, not weak-label fine-tuning. No PGR is computed, but strong-model DPO on the true preference data is reported and works as a ceiling analogue. The study does not compare against naive weak-label fine-tuning, so V2 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude WSPO transfers alignment from a weak aligned model to a stronger one and amplifies it, beating DPO while preserving the strong model's reasoning and knowledge. They do not explain the amplification. The vision-language result is a short appendix demonstration.
record.recipe_differences: WSPO optimizes a loss matching the strong model's log-probability change to the weak model's pre/post-alignment distribution difference. It does not fine-tune the strong model on labels generated by the weak supervisor, and it reports benchmark outcomes rather than PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with gamma: in the same-model Arena-Hard analysis, gamma 1.0 is nearly identical to DPO, while gamma 0.5 and 0.1 yield higher scores. The paper also reports a modest gain when transferring directly from a base model without the SFT phase. In the length-reward task, it describes WSPO as performing better than PPO at lower temperatures.

fits_no_version.finding: The WSPO student often exceeds the strong model trained by DPO on the same true preference data, i.e. the weak signal beats the strong-ceiling analogue.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-to-strong transfer of alignment signals can exceed direct strong-model training on the same preferences (PGR>1 relative to a DPO ceiling).

record.problems: No PGR values or true-label strong ceilings are reported, so the paper does not quantify recovered gap. Many benchmark comparisons use automatic judges; the authors note human evaluation is often not reproducible. Most benchmark tables do not report uncertainty. The paper says it did not conduct an in-depth dataset evaluation or account for safety, honesty, and related considerations in designing WSPO.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the common-sense and reasoning benchmark scores in Table 2 because they assess preservation of general capabilities rather than weak-to-strong alignment performance. Also omitted extensive DPO hyperparameter sweep values and SimPO comparisons in Appendix F where they compare other methods rather than directly measure the weak-supervisor transfer effect. Figure 4's gamma and weak-model-size plots are not transcribed because their numeric values are not stated.

untested.parts: Ordinary fine-tuning on weak-model labels; PGR with a true-label strong ceiling (strong DPO is only an analogue).
Entirely. No naive weak-to-strong baseline, no auxiliary confidence loss, no ensembling.
Representation predictors of PGR; chess and reward modelling tasks; systematic size sweeps with numbers (Figure 4 is not quantified).
Entirely. The reward reparameterization is not a student-beats-supervisor condition.
Vision classification; weak-supervisor scores on MMHal-Bench.

missing.what: Llama3.2-1B SimPO-aligned supervisor (Arena-Hard 14.60) transferred via WSPO to Llama3.2-3B (31.20 vs SFT 29.60) and Llama3.1-8B (52.60 vs SFT 50.30). Bears on V1 and on student-size dependence.
WSPO transfer from a SimPO-aligned same-size Llama3-8B: 53.80 vs SimPO 52.20 vs SFT 38.90.
Qwen2-7B-Base WSPO on AlpacaEval 2 (LC 26.77, WR 26.68) and MT-Bench 7.00, against weak 1.5B-Base DPO scores of 5.56, 4.79 and 5.03.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Comparator rows for weak and strong baselines were relinked to none; their values belong in the baselines of the WSPO rows. r15 mixed the LC and raw win-rate columns from the flattened Table 1. Comparisons to the weak supervisor are inflated by the student's capability, and no true-label ceiling PGR is computed.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not use ordinary fine-tuning on weak-model labels, compute PGR, or report a strong ceiling trained on true labels.
The paper compares WSPO with SFT and DPO on alignment benchmarks, but does not compute PGR or test auxiliary confidence loss or ensembling weak supervisors.
It reports alignment results across model sizes, tasks, and some model families, but does not measure PGR or test which representations predict it.
No reported test of exploiting what a weak supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, or error similarity.
The paper gives a reward-representation derivation, not conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
Vision-language preference alignment is evaluated, but no PGR is reported.
